    The Debrief With Mario Parker: Trump Hits Trail To Persuade Anxious Voters
    Bloomberg's Mario Parker joins for the Debrief to discuss President Donald Trump’s red-state campaign push, concerns among Republicans about his role on the trail and the party’s difficult midterm environment. He speaks with Kailey Leinz and Joe Mathieu on Bloomberg’s "Balance of Power." (Source: Bloomberg)
    US May Send Third Carrier Strike Group to Middle East
    The Pentagon may send a third aircraft carrier and 10,000 sailors and Marines to the Persian Gulf, within striking distance of Iran. The USS Theodore Roosevelt has left San Diego, but we don't know its final destination. Kate Sullivan reports from the White House on "Balance of Power." (Source: Bloomberg)
    There Is No End Game in Iran, Dalton Says
    Bale Dalton, a Democratic congressional candidate from Florida, says sending the USS Theodore Roosevelt toward the Middle East, will only deepen the conflict with Iran. He speaks on "Balance of Power." (Source: Bloomberg)
    Hill Says FDIC Won’t Rule Out Agentic AI Bank-Run Risk
    Travis Hill, FDIC chairman, says the agency is not ruling out risks from AI tools that could allow customers to move deposits more quickly in search of higher returns, though he says such a scenario would require a significant shift in how customers delegate financial decisions. Hill also says there is a “strong case” for expanding deposit insurance coverage, either by raising the current limit or creating a category of accounts with higher coverage. He speaks with Kailey Leinz and Joe Mathieu on Bloomberg’s "Balance of Power." (Source: Bloomberg)
    Dalton: We’ve Gotten Ourselves Into a Forever War
    Bale Dalton, US Navy Reserve Captain, Democratic Nominee for Florida's 7th Congressional and former NASA Chief of Staff, says the war with Iran has become a “forever war” with no strategic value or defined end state. Dalton says deploying a third aircraft carrier strike group to the Middle East puts more US service members in harm’s way and argues the conflict is making the country more vulnerable. He speaks with Kailey Leinz and Joe Mathieu on Bloomberg’s "Balance of Power." (Source: Bloomberg)
    Brouillette Says Diesel Export Ban Would Be a Bad Idea
    Dan Brouillette, Former Secretary of Energy during the first Trump administration and Co-chair of the Torridon Group, says a US diesel export ban would be a “bad idea” because it could eventually force refiners to cut production and raise gasoline prices. Brouillette says reopening the Strait of Hormuz is the most important near-term step to bringing fuel prices down and argues markets need confidence that it will remain open. Brouillette thinks constrained US refining capacity is contributing to diesel scarcity and remains a longer-term infrastructure problem. He speaks with Kailey Leinz and Joe Mathieu on Bloomberg’s "Balance of Power." (Source: Bloomberg)

    The Guardian view on the death penalty: Christa Pike’s execution was botched, but cruelty is inherent | Editorial
    Three-quarters of nations have rightly abolished capital punishment in law or practice, but killing by the state has surged in the US What is the kindest way to kill? That’s the question being asked once more following Tennessee’s failed attempts to execute Christa Pike for the brutal murder of a classmate, Colleen Slemmer, when she was 18. The 50-year-old was taken to a medical facility, her condition unknown, with witnesses describing her snoring loudly around 40 minutes after receiving two injections of pentobarbital on Wednesday. It is the second botched killing in months, prompting Tennessee’s governor to order a halt to executions. Lethal injection was supposed to be the humane alternative to firing squads and electric chairs. They in turn were seen as an improvement on hanging, which looked much like lynching in a system disproportionately handing the death penalty to black men. The age and ill health of those executed, and the ethical refusal of most medical staff to be involved, may contribute to botched injections. But analysis of autopsy results has provided compelling evidence that suffering is inherent; injections – especially those involving paralytic drugs – have merely disguised it. What is described as safeguarding the dignity of prisoners is really about reducing the discomfort of witnesses who would otherwise see their suffering.     The horror of the Cornell rape case is how ordinary it is | Moira Donegan
    Many men rape; many men giggle encouragingly, or shrug indifferently, when their friends rape. Many men rape, and few seem to think that it’s a very big deal Maybe more than anything else, sexual violence is repetitive. Men commit it in patterns: mostly against women who are close by and vulnerable, just below them on some social hierarchy: their assistant, their date, their friend, their daughter, their student, their kid’s babysitter. Men rape for opportunity – because they can – and for status – because it makes them feel good. They rape to impress other men, documenting it on phones for one another’s benefit. Men rape and do not always seem to register much of a difference between the sex they’ve had that was rape and the sex that they’ve had that wasn’t. They rape, often, without seeming to think about it, registering their victims’ unwillingness with vague contempt, if at all.     How Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptations
    There’s no Leon, Claire or Ada Wong in Cregger’s adaptation. Instead, it re-creates something more fundamental – the strange, terrifying experience of actually playing the game • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here I’ve been surprised by the number of Resident Evil fans complaining on social media about Zach Cregger’s cinematic adaptation of the survival horror series. “It’s not a real Resident Evil movie,” they’ve claimed. Were we watching the same film? Certainly, it doesn’t feature any of the familiar heroes – there’s no Leon, no Claire, no Ada Wong – and there’s a distinct lack of recognisable antagonists and well-known locations. Despite all of this, Cregger’s interpretation is one of the most accurate and interesting video game films ever made. On the surface, it’s about a zombifying virus that gets accidentally released in Raccoon City by the Umbrella Corporation. These are, of course, the foundations of the Resi mythos. More interestingly, Cregger seeks to replicate and explore the structural and narrative conventions of the series. In the film, the player character, hapless courier Bryan Hodukavich, is thrust into a viral outbreak, with no weapons and no idea what’s going on. He is then submerged into an uncanny shadow world of escalating peril and body horror. The film takes us through a series of locations dragged straight from the games – an abandoned farmhouse, a road tunnel crammed with abandoned cars, a hospital and the obligatory sewer level. As he progresses, Bryan finds increasingly powerful weapons, from a handgun to an assault rifle – but he is always short on ammo. And there are typewriters in at least two scenes!
